headline: No model came close to arcade speed. Jev, the better of two System-1 decision models, won 1 game in 3 at 10% and at 15% of full speed and none faster; Microsoft-Decision-1 and a local Gemma 4 E2B never won at any speed, because they hardly move the cannon.
finding_1: Speed caps play even with perfect judgement. A coded player has to decide every 0.115 game seconds to win half its games. At Jev's 0.49 s, Microsoft-Decision-1's 0.58 s and Gemma's 0.21 s per decision, that caps the game at about 23%, 20% and 54% of full speed. Full speed needs a decision in about 0.1 s of real time, roughly five times faster than the fastest System-1 model over the network.
finding_2: Inside that cap, judgement decided the games. On 200 situations from real play, Jev chose a sound move 77% of the time; it lost games by running out of lives, dodging 36 of 50 bombs. Microsoft-Decision-1 chose well 28% of the time: it waited in 132 of 200 situations and never dodged. Gemma 4 E2B fired in all 200, so it only hit aliens that passed over it, 12 of 18 in every game.
finding_3: It was cheap. 14,238 model decisions over 26 games, plus about 700 quality and latency questions, cost $0.21 in total ($0.17 Jev, $0.04 Microsoft-Decision-1, local Gemma free): about $0.00002 per Jev decision and $0.000007 per Decision-1 decision. Cost is not what stops decision models playing in real time; latency and judgement are.
